LESSON MENU
RC CIRCUIT TRANSIENTS
RC circuit transients occur when the voltage across a capacitor changes.
DISCUSSION
A transient is the relation between a change in current and a change in applied voltage.
If there is no change in the applied voltage, no current flows.
If there is no change in the applied voltage, there is no current.
If there is no change in the applied voltage, no current flows.If there is no change in the applied voltage, no current flows.
When DC is applied to an RC circuit, the capacitor begins to charge at a rate determined by T = R x C. This is the time constant for any given RC circuit.
If the DC input is applied for one time constant, the capacitor charges to 0.63 x applied voltage.
It takes 5 time constants to fully charge the capacitor to the applied voltage.
Likewise, if the applied voltage drops to 0, it takes 5 time constants to fully discharge the capacitor.
The process of instantaneously applying constant DC and then abruptly dropping the voltage to zero is a square wave input.
The output Ec waveform is made up of the charging and discharging curves for a capacitor. Its frequency is equal to that of the input square wave.

There are many useful applications for RC circuits. A camera uses an RC circuit to fire a flash bulb.
With S1 in the charge position, C1 charges through R1. It takes 5 time constants (2 seconds) to charge to the applied voltage.
The charging current is maximum at the beginning of charge. Since the capacitor appears as a short the first instant, maximum current is 2 mA.
When the shutter is opened, S1 allows C1 to discharge through the flashbulb. Its resistance is low compared to R1. The RC time constant is very short.
It takes 5 time constants (0.001 seconds) for C1 to discharge through the small resistance of the bulb.
Notice the extremely high current that is produced at the beginning of discharge. The battery in a camera is only capable of supplying low current.
Another application of the RC time constant is found in coupling capacitors.
Coupling capacitors are used to pass only the AC component of pulsating DC.
In this circuit, the input is a 10 Vpp signal "riding" on a 5 VDC level.
C1 will charge to the average DC level of 5 VDC. If the input remains at this level, no current flows and as a result, the voltage drop across R1 is zero.
C1 will charge to the average DC level of 5 VDC. If the input remains at this level, there is no flow of charge and as a result, the voltage drop across R1 is zero.
C1 will charge to the average DC level of 5 VDC. If the input remains at this level, no current flows and as a result, the voltage drop across R1 is zero. g
If the input increases or decreases, charge or discharge current will result. Since these currents are in opposite directions, AC is the result across R1.
All of the AC component and none of the DC component is dropped across R1. All of the DC component and none of the AC component is dropped across C1.
For coupling capacitors to work, a long time constant is required so that C1 has little time to charge and discharge with input variations (AC component)..nt).
A short time constant would cause C1 to have capacitive reactance and some of the AC signal would be dropped across C1.
